title: Khatm: the whole book
hook: finishing a whole reading, often in Ramadan, with a gathering

segments.voice: Yesterday, handling the mushaf: purity to touch it, a high place, never the trash. Your line was keep it high.

It's late on one of the last nights of Ramadan. The mosque is fuller than it's been all month. Children are awake long past their bedtimes. The imam is reciting An-Nas, the very last surah, and in some mosques, when he finishes, he goes straight back and recites the opening of the book again. Then comes a long supplication. Some people are weeping; others are already handing out sweets. The whole book, finished.
screen: `A LATE NIGHT IN RAMADAN.` → `THE LAST SURAH, THEN THE FIRST.` → `WEEPING, AND SWEETS.`

segments.voice: Khatm means a seal, a finishing. It's the same root as khatam, seal, in the title the Qur'an gives the Prophet ﷺ in Surah 33: the seal of the prophets. For the Qur'an, a khatm is one complete reading, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas. Ramadan is its season. The hadith collections say the angel Jibril went over the whole Qur'an with the Prophet every Ramadan, and twice in the year he died. So Ramadan is when a full reading is most often attempted, alone at home, or by hearing it across the nights of tarawih, often a juz' a night. When a mosque reaches the end, there's often a gathering, with a special supplication after the last surah, the du'a of khatm, often long and often tearful. A report says the companion Anas ibn Malik, when he finished the Qur'an, would gather his family and make du'a with them. Customs vary. In some places a child's first khatm is celebrated with a party and new clothes: in parts of South Asia it's called an Ameen, in Turkey a hatim. And some readers who finish An-Nas begin again at once from al-Fatiha, so the reading never really stops. How often? You met one hadith in the week of the thirty parts: once a month, and not faster than seven days. Another says the one who finishes in less than three days hasn't understood it. So speed isn't the point. A page a day is slow, and it still arrives. The point is the whole: not only the parts you love, but every page, once.
screen: `KHATM: A SEAL, A FINISHING` · `RAMADAN IS ITS SEASON` · `A GATHERING, A SUPPLICATION` · `BEGIN AGAIN FROM AL-FATIHA`

segments.voice: Ask what pace is true for you: a juz' a day, a page a day, a few verses a day, or one reciter heard through the whole book. Pick an amount you could keep on a bad day, not only a good one, and hold that plan quietly. If you're here to learn about the path rather than practice it, choose a translation of the meanings and a pace.
Khatm. A seal: one complete reading of the Qur'an, from al-Fatiha to An-Nas, often finished in Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: the whole book, once. However long it takes, the whole book arrives. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Muslims complete a full reading of the Qur'an in Ramadan, at home or through the tarawih prayers, and mosques and families often mark a khatm with a gathering, a special supplication and food.
